explanations.answer: Look at the Lamb of God
explanations.explanation: John the Baptist sees Jesus walking by and says, “Look, the Lamb of God!” He says it to two of his own disciples, and they're standing close enough to hear every word. The day before, John said something close to that, calling Jesus “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). If it were me, I'd have just yelled “Hey, it's Him!” and tripped over my own base.

explanations.answer: Look at the Lion of Judah
explanations.explanation: I get why a big title like that came to mind, friend. But that's not what John says. His words are “Look, the Lamb of God!” Those two disciples are right there, and that's the title they hear.

explanations.answer: Look at the Son of David
explanations.explanation: That's a title that shows up elsewhere in the Gospels, so I see why it came to mind. But John doesn't use it here. What he says is “Look, the Lamb of God!” That's the line that gets two disciples moving.

Not quite, friend. The text says that when the two disciples heard John say it, they followed Jesus. They heard the words and their feet started moving. John said four little words, and two people were already on their way.
That's right, baker. John says, “Look, the Lamb of God!” and the two disciples who hear it follow Jesus. No staying put, no meeting about it. They hear it and they go.

You got it, baker. Jesus asks, “What do you want?” and they answer with a question of their own: “Rabbi, where are You staying?” They call Him Rabbi, which means Teacher. Jesus asks them what they want and they ask for His address. Honestly, that's an answer I respect.

Close, baker, since it's a where question. But they don't ask about what's next. They ask, “where are You staying?” It's a smaller question than the one you picked, and Jesus has a very simple answer for it.
They do call Him Rabbi, which means Teacher, so I see how you got here. But they never ask about a lesson time. They ask, “where are You staying?” No schedule, no appointment, just a where.

That's right, friend. They went, they saw where He was staying, and they spent that day with Him. The text adds that it was about the tenth hour. Whatever time they showed up, they didn't just peek in and leave.
Not this time, friend. The text says they went and saw where Jesus was staying, and they spent that day with Him. They went along when He said “Come and see,” and they stayed.

Yes, baker. Andrew first finds his brother Simon and tells him, “We have found the Messiah.” Andrew is the one who heard John's testimony and followed Jesus. He had news, and the first stop was family. I bet he walked fast.
Not quite, friend. The text says Andrew first found his brother Simon. Andrew is Simon Peter's brother, so this was a family visit. The first person he went looking for was Simon.

Right on, baker. Andrew doesn't just tell Simon the news, he brings him to Jesus. Then Jesus looks at Simon, and that's where the story goes next. Andrew could have just texted, friend. He walked his brother over instead.

explanations.answer: Takes Simon to John the Baptist
explanations.explanation: I see why you picked it, since John is the one who pointed Andrew to Jesus. But the text says Andrew brought Simon to Jesus. Simon doesn't meet John here. His next meeting is with Jesus.
Nope, baker. Andrew doesn't send Simon anywhere. He brings him to Jesus himself. And that's a big difference, because Andrew goes along.

Yes, baker! Jesus says, “You will be called Cephas,” which is translated as Peter. Notice that Jesus says it right after looking at Simon and calling him by his name and his father's name. A whole new name, and Simon hasn't even said a word yet.

Barnabas is a real name from the Bible, but it belongs to someone else. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, was called Barnabas by the apostles, and it means Son of Encouragement (Acts 4:36). The new name for Simon is “Cephas,” which is translated as Peter.

That's a fun one, and it's a real name. Jesus gave it to the brothers James and John, and it means “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). But that's a different pair of brothers. Simon's new name is “Cephas.”
That's it, baker. Jesus finds Philip and says, “Follow Me.” Just two words, and Philip is the one He says them to. Short and sweet. Honestly, my instructions for a cookie batch take longer than that.
Waiting is a real thing people do, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He tells Philip, “Follow Me.” Nobody is told to stay put in this verse. It's an invitation to come along.
I see why meet came to mind, since Jesus has just found him. But the word is “Follow.” Jesus tells Philip, “Follow Me.” It's an invitation to come along.

Yes, baker. Philip tells Nathanael, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law.” Moses was Israel's leader, and the Law is what he wrote. Philip adds that this is the One the prophets foretold, too. Philip had a lot to say, and he got it all out in one breath.

Actually it's true, friend. Philip says, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Philip points right back to what he wrote. Then Philip adds, “the One the prophets foretold.”

explanations.answer: Can anything good come from Nazareth
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Nathanael asks, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip doesn't argue with him, he just says, “Come and see.” Philip had a good answer, and it was an invitation.

explanations.answer: Where in the world is Nazareth
explanations.explanation: That would be a fair question, but it's not the one Nathanael asks. He seems to know Nazareth already. What he asks is, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” It's a question about the place, not its address.

Interesting guess, baker, but Jerusalem never comes up in this conversation. Nathanael's question is about Nazareth itself: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” And Philip's answer is just two words, “Come and see.”

That's right, baker. Jesus sees Nathanael coming and says, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” Nathanael hasn't said a word to Jesus yet. Jesus speaks first, and what He says is kind.

Actually it's true, friend. When Jesus sees Nathanael approaching, He says, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” That's what Jesus says about him, before Nathanael has said anything at all.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.” Nathanael asked how Jesus knew him, and that was the answer. Think about it, friend. If somebody told me they saw me before I was even called, I'd check my apron for a hidden camera.
The Jordan is in this chapter, since John was baptizing at Bethany beyond the Jordan (John 1:28). But Jesus doesn't put Nathanael there. He says, “I saw you under the fig tree.” The place is a tree.
That's a guess from a different story, baker. Jesus doesn't mention a gate or a city. He says, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.” So Nathanael was under a tree.

explanations.answer: He calls Jesus the Son of God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Nathanael answers, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” A moment earlier he was asking about Nazareth. That's quite a turn. And it all comes right after Jesus tells him what He saw.

explanations.answer: He says Philip must have told Him
explanations.explanation: That's a very human guess, I'll give you that. But Nathanael doesn't say it. He answers, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” No theories, just that.

explanations.answer: He asks Jesus for a bigger sign
explanations.explanation: I see where that comes from, since Jesus does say bigger things are coming. But Nathanael doesn't ask for anything. He just says, “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Then Jesus is the one who talks about greater things (John 1:50).

Not quite, friend. Jesus asks, “Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree?” and then says, “You will see greater things than these.” So the fig tree isn't the biggest thing. There's more coming.
That's right, baker. Jesus doesn't call the fig tree the biggest thing. He says, “You will see greater things than these.” Even something that amazing is just the start.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). Notice He says “you will all see,” so He's speaking to more than just Nathanael.

Tongues of fire do show up later in the Bible, when they appear on the believers at Pentecost (Acts 2:3). But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says it's “the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

A bright cloud does appear in the Gospels, on the mountain where a voice speaks from it (Matthew 17:5). But that's not what Jesus says here. In this verse He says, “the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
